chapters.summary: The Dashwood family has long lived at Norland Park in Sussex. When the old owner dies, his will ties the estate to his nephew Henry Dashwood's son and grandson, leaving little for Henry's second wife, Mrs. Dashwood, and their daughters. Henry dies a year later, having made his son by his first marriage, John Dashwood, promise to help them. John privately means to give his three half-sisters a thousand pounds each. His wife, Fanny, arrives straight after the funeral and takes over the house. Mrs. Dashwood is so offended that only her eldest daughter, the sensible nineteen-year-old Elinor, persuades her to stay. The other daughters are passionate Marianne and thirteen-year-old Margaret.

Fanny Dashwood, John Dashwood's wife, is now mistress of Norland, and Mrs. Dashwood, John's stepmother, stays on with her daughters as guests while she looks for a house nearby. Fanny objects to John's plan of giving his half-sisters three thousand pounds, saying it would rob their little son Harry. In one long conversation she talks him down step by step: first to five hundred pounds each, then to a yearly allowance for their mother, then to occasional small presents. In the end John decides that his promise to his dying father only meant neighbourly help, such as assistance with moving and gifts of fish and game, and that giving money is unnecessary.

Mrs. Dashwood and her daughters remain at Norland for about six months while she looks for a house she can afford. Her dislike of her daughter-in-law Fanny grows. Fanny's brother, Edward Ferrars, comes to stay: a shy, plain, quiet young man, eldest son of a rich family, whose mother and sister want him to make a figure in the world, though he prefers a quiet private life. He and Elinor, the eldest Dashwood daughter, grow attached. Mrs. Dashwood warms to him and expects a wedding soon. Marianne, the second daughter, not yet seventeen, likes Edward but finds him spiritless, complaining that he read Cowper aloud without feeling.

Marianne Dashwood regrets that Edward Ferrars has no taste for drawing; her sister Elinor defends his taste, sense and goodness. Pressed, Elinor admits that she thinks highly of him and likes him, and Marianne is indignant at such cool words. Elinor explains that they are not engaged: she is unsure how much Edward cares, he is sometimes low-spirited, and he depends on his mother, who expects him to marry well. Edward's sister, Fanny Dashwood, notices the attachment and pointedly tells Mrs. Dashwood about the family's great expectations for him. Offended, Mrs. Dashwood wants to leave at once. A letter then arrives from a relative of hers, a wealthy gentleman in Devonshire, offering a cottage on his estate at a low rent, and she accepts.

Mrs. Dashwood tells her stepson John Dashwood and his wife Fanny that she has taken a house in Devonshire: Barton Cottage, four miles north of Exeter, offered by her relative Sir John Middleton. Edward Ferrars, Fanny's brother, is surprised and concerned at the distance. She invites them all to visit, Edward most warmly, to show she ignores Fanny's objections to him and Elinor. John is sorry the distance prevents him helping with the move; Fanny resents seeing the family's china, linen, books and Marianne's pianoforte sent away. The horses and carriage are sold on Elinor's advice and the household is cut to three servants. John gives them no money. After tearful farewells, with Marianne mourning aloud for Norland, they leave.

Mrs. Dashwood and her daughters Elinor, Marianne and Margaret arrive at Barton Cottage in Devonshire. It is small but comfortable and set in a pleasant valley among hills; Mrs. Dashwood plans improvements she cannot yet afford, and they arrange their books, Marianne's pianoforte and Elinor's drawings. The next day their landlord and relative Sir John Middleton calls from Barton Park: a good-humoured, friendly man of about forty who presses them to dine at the park and sends presents of garden produce and game. His wife, Lady Middleton, visits the day after. She is handsome and elegant, about twenty-six, but reserved and cold with little to say; her six-year-old son supplies the conversation. They promise to dine at the park.

Mrs. Dashwood and her daughters dine at Barton Park, half a mile from their cottage. Their host Sir John Middleton, a sportsman who loves company, and his wife Lady Middleton, who cares for her elegant table and her children, entertain constantly. There they meet Mrs. Jennings, Lady Middleton's mother, a merry, talkative, rather vulgar elderly woman who jokes about lovers and husbands, and Colonel Brandon, Sir John's friend, a quiet, serious, gentlemanly man past thirty-five. In the evening Marianne Dashwood plays and sings. Sir John applauds loudly while talking through every song, and Lady Middleton asks for one just sung. Only Colonel Brandon listens with silent attention, which Marianne respects, though she thinks him old.

Mrs. Jennings, Lady Middleton's mother and a widow who loves matchmaking, decides that Colonel Brandon, Sir John Middleton's friend, is in love with Marianne Dashwood, and teases them both. Marianne thinks it absurd and unkind: at thirty-five he seems to her an old man, fit only for flannel waistcoats, who complains of rheumatism. Her mother, Mrs. Dashwood, and her sister Elinor laugh at her notions of age and marriage. When Elinor leaves the room, Marianne tells her mother she fears Edward Ferrars must be ill, since after nearly a fortnight he has not come to Barton. She wonders at how cold and calm his farewell to Elinor was, and at Elinor's composure.

The Dashwoods settle at Barton Cottage, seeing few people beyond Barton Park. Out walking on the downs with her younger sister Margaret, Marianne Dashwood is caught in driving rain, runs downhill, falls and twists her ankle. A young gentleman out shooting with his dogs picks her up and carries her home. Handsome and graceful, he gives his name as Willoughby, staying at Allenham, and asks leave to call next day. Marianne and her mother are full of admiration. Sir John Middleton, their landlord, calls and says Willoughby is a fine shot and rider who visits yearly an old lady at Allenham Court whose property he will inherit, and has an estate of his own in Somersetshire. He teases Marianne about setting her cap at him.

Willoughby, the young man who carried Marianne Dashwood home, calls the next morning and is warmly received. He and Marianne find they share the same tastes in music, dancing and books, and talk like old friends. He visits every day; they read, talk and sing together, and her mother, Mrs. Dashwood, soon hopes for a marriage. Her sister Elinor likes him but notes that he says what he thinks too freely, with little caution. Elinor now sees that Colonel Brandon, Sir John Middleton's quiet friend, really does care for Marianne, and pities him. Willoughby and Marianne mock Brandon as dull, a man everyone praises and nobody cares about, while Elinor defends his sense, good breeding and kindness.

The Dashwoods are drawn into a round of parties, dances and outings arranged by Sir John Middleton at Barton Park. Willoughby is always included, and he and Marianne Dashwood show their attachment openly: she sees no one else, and they dance and talk only with each other. Elinor wishes her sister would be more guarded, but Marianne scorns concealment and their mother sees no harm. Elinor herself is less happy, missing the companion she left at Norland, and finds only Colonel Brandon, Sir John's friend, worth talking to. One evening he asks her about Marianne's belief that no one can love twice, and lets fall that he once knew a lady very like her, then stops short, leaving Elinor to suspect an old attachment.

Marianne Dashwood tells her sister Elinor that Willoughby has given her a horse. Elinor points out that they cannot afford to keep it and that the gift is improper, and Marianne reluctantly refuses it. Willoughby answers that the horse, Queen Mab, is still hers, calling her by her first name, and Elinor concludes they must be engaged. Their younger sister Margaret reports seeing him cut off a lock of Marianne's hair and kiss it. At Barton Park, Mrs. Jennings, Lady Middleton's mother, presses Margaret to name Elinor's admirer, and Margaret lets out that his name begins with F. A pleasure party is planned for the next day to a fine estate twelve miles off belonging to Colonel Brandon's brother-in-law.

The party gathers at Barton Park for the outing to Whitwell. At breakfast Colonel Brandon, Sir John Middleton's friend, receives a letter, changes colour, and says he must leave for London at once on business; without him Whitwell cannot be visited. He refuses to explain or delay and rides away. Mrs. Jennings, Sir John's mother-in-law, whispers to Elinor Dashwood that it must concern a Miss Williams, who she says is the colonel's natural daughter. The party drives about the country instead. Willoughby takes Marianne Dashwood off alone in his curricle, and Mrs. Jennings finds out that he showed her over Allenham, the house of his elderly relative Mrs. Smith. Elinor calls this improper; Marianne at first defends it, then half admits it was unwise.

Mrs. Jennings, mother-in-law of Sir John Middleton, spends days guessing why Colonel Brandon left so suddenly for London. Elinor Dashwood wonders more at the silence of her sister Marianne and Willoughby, who behave like an engaged couple but tell no one; she supposes his small income and expensive habits may delay a marriage. Willoughby spends nearly all his time at Barton Cottage. One evening, about a week after the colonel's departure, he protests against Mrs. Dashwood's plan to improve the cottage, declaring it perfect, and makes her promise never to alter it or her family's kindness to him. He agrees to dine with them the next day at four.

Mrs. Dashwood and two of her daughters call at Barton Park, leaving Marianne at home. Returning, they find Marianne running upstairs in tears and Willoughby, her constant visitor, in distress. He says his relative Mrs. Smith of Allenham is sending him to London on business at once, and that he does not expect to return to Devonshire soon. Embarrassed, he will not accept Mrs. Dashwood's invitation to come back to the cottage, and hurries away. Mrs. Dashwood decides Mrs. Smith disapproves of the match and that the couple are secretly engaged. Elinor, the eldest daughter, is uneasy: she believes he loves Marianne but wants proof of an engagement. Marianne can neither eat nor speak and weeps all evening.

Marianne Dashwood gives herself up to grief after Willoughby's departure: she does not sleep, walks alone, and plays the music they shared. No letter comes from him. Her sister Elinor urges their mother to ask Marianne directly whether she is engaged, but Mrs. Dashwood refuses to force her confidence. About a week later, walking with her sisters, Marianne sees a rider and is sure it is Willoughby. It is Edward Ferrars, brother of their sister-in-law Fanny and the man Elinor cares for, coming to visit. He admits he has been in Devonshire a fortnight, staying with friends near Plymouth. He is cold and low-spirited and says little; Elinor is hurt but treats him as a family friend.

Edward Ferrars, the Dashwoods' guest at Barton Cottage, is warmed by Mrs. Dashwood's welcome but remains out of spirits. After dinner the family talk by the fire. Edward says he has no wish for the public distinction his mother, Mrs. Ferrars, wants for him. Marianne Dashwood declares that money has little to do with happiness, then names two thousand a year as a bare competence, which makes her sister Elinor laugh. They imagine how each would spend a fortune, and Edward teases Marianne about books, music and her belief that nobody loves twice. They discuss shyness and manners. When Marianne calls Edward reserved he is startled and agitated, and falls silent and gloomy.

Edward Ferrars, visiting the Dashwoods at Barton Cottage, remains low-spirited, and Elinor Dashwood cannot tell whether he still cares for her. After a morning walk he praises the country in plain terms, teasing Marianne Dashwood by saying he knows nothing of the picturesque. Marianne notices that he wears a ring holding a plait of hair and asks if it is his sister Fanny's; he blushes and says it is. Both sisters privately believe the hair is Elinor's, though Elinor knows she never gave it. Sir John Middleton, their landlord, and his mother-in-law Mrs. Jennings call, discover that Ferrars begins with F, and invite everyone to the park. Hearing them tease Marianne, Edward learns of Willoughby and gently jokes with her about him.

Edward Ferrars leaves Barton Cottage after a week, melancholy and with no fixed plans; he regrets that his mother, Mrs. Ferrars, and he never agreed on a profession, so that he is idle and dependent. Elinor Dashwood controls her sadness by keeping busy at her drawing, which her sister Marianne cannot understand. Soon after, Sir John and Lady Middleton and Mrs. Jennings bring new visitors to the cottage: Mrs. Jennings's younger daughter Charlotte and her husband, Mr. and Mrs. Palmer, who arrived unexpectedly the night before. Mrs. Palmer is pretty, plump, expecting a child, and laughs at everything; Mr. Palmer is grave and rude, reads the newspaper and ignores her. The Dashwood sisters are pressed to dine at the park next day.

Elinor and Marianne Dashwood spend the day at Barton Park with the Palmers, the daughter and son-in-law of Mrs. Jennings. Charlotte Palmer chatters and laughs, urging the sisters to come to London in winter and to her house, Cleveland, at Christmas; they decline. Mr. Palmer, who is standing for Parliament, grumbles at the weather and contradicts everyone, which his wife finds droll. Hoping for news of Willoughby, whose estate Combe Magna is in the same county as Cleveland, Elinor questions Mrs. Palmer. She barely knows him but says everyone likes him, and that all London is saying he will marry Marianne: she heard it confirmed, she thinks, by Colonel Brandon, whom she met in Bond Street.

The Palmers leave for Cleveland. Sir John Middleton and his mother-in-law Mrs. Jennings then meet in Exeter two young women who prove to be Mrs. Jennings's relations, and invite them to Barton Park: Anne Steele, nearly thirty, plain and foolish, always talking of beaux, and her younger sister Lucy Steele, pretty and sharp but uneducated. Both flatter Lady Middleton by doting on her spoiled children. Elinor and Marianne Dashwood are taken to meet them and do not care to know them better, but Sir John throws them together and tells the Steeles all about Marianne's suitor and Elinor's, whispering the name Ferrars. Anne says she knows Mr. Ferrars very well; Lucy corrects her, saying they met him at their uncle's.

Lucy Steele, the younger of the two sisters staying at Barton Park, seeks out Elinor Dashwood's company. Walking to the cottage, she asks about Mrs. Ferrars, the mother of Elinor's sister-in-law, and then confides, as a great secret, that she has been engaged for four years to the elder son, Edward Ferrars. They met when he was a pupil of her uncle, Mr. Pratt, at Longstaple near Plymouth. Elinor cannot believe it, but Lucy shows his miniature and a letter in his handwriting, says he had just been with them before visiting Barton, and that the ring he wears holds her hair. She asks Elinor to keep the secret. Elinor hides her feelings, shocked and wretched.

Elinor Dashwood thinks over what Lucy Steele has told her and can no longer doubt that Edward Ferrars is engaged to Lucy. She believes he formed the tie as a boy of nineteen, now loves herself, and will be unhappy with an uneducated, calculating wife; she grieves more for him than for herself. She resolves to tell neither her mother nor her sister Marianne, and hides her distress. Wanting to learn more and to show Lucy she is not wounded, she looks for a private talk. At a dull evening at Barton Park, while Lady Middleton and the others play cards and Marianne goes to the pianoforte, Elinor offers to help Lucy finish a filigree basket for Lady Middleton's little daughter.

Working beside Lucy Steele at Barton Park while Marianne Dashwood plays the pianoforte, Elinor Dashwood reopens the subject of Lucy's secret engagement to Edward Ferrars. Lucy says Edward has only two thousand pounds and depends on his proud mother, Mrs. Ferrars, who if angered might settle everything on his brother Robert, so they must wait. Her plan is for Edward to become a clergyman, and she asks Elinor to persuade her brother John Dashwood to give him the Norland living. Elinor declines, and refuses to advise whether the engagement should be broken off. Lucy pointedly hints at Elinor's own interest and is glad she will not be in London. They part no better friends. The Steeles stay on at the park.

Mrs. Jennings, Lady Middleton's mother, who has a house in London near Portman Square, invites Elinor and Marianne Dashwood to spend the winter with her there. Elinor declines, not wishing to leave their mother, but Marianne is eager, and Elinor sees she longs to be where Willoughby is. Mrs. Dashwood insists both go, expecting much pleasure for them and saying Elinor may get to know her sister-in-law's family; Elinor answers that she likes Edward Ferrars but is indifferent to the rest. Elinor agrees, unwilling to leave Marianne to her own guidance. The sisters leave Barton with Mrs. Jennings in the first week of January; the Middletons are to follow, and the Miss Steeles stay at the park meanwhile.

Elinor and Marianne Dashwood travel three days to London with Mrs. Jennings, the Middletons' talkative mother, and settle in her comfortable London house. Marianne is silent on the road and writes at once to Willoughby, which convinces Elinor they must be engaged. That evening a knock makes Marianne sure he has come, but the visitor is Colonel Brandon, the Middletons' friend who left Barton suddenly; she leaves the room and he asks, concerned, whether she is ill. Next morning Charlotte Palmer, Mrs. Jennings's daughter, calls and takes them shopping in Bond Street, where Marianne watches for Willoughby. No visit or letter comes. Elinor resolves to write to their mother if matters do not improve.

In London with Mrs. Jennings, Marianne Dashwood decides the mild weather is keeping Willoughby in the country hunting, and watches for frost. Colonel Brandon, their friend from Barton, calls almost daily to talk with her sister Elinor. About a week after their arrival Willoughby leaves his card while they are out, but he does not return or answer Marianne's notes, and he stays away from a dance given by Sir John and Lady Middleton, now also in town, though invited. Elinor writes urging their mother to ask Marianne how things stand. Colonel Brandon then asks Elinor whether Marianne's engagement to Willoughby, talked of everywhere, is settled; Elinor says she believes they are attached, and he leaves wishing Marianne happiness.

For several days Willoughby neither calls nor writes. Elinor and Marianne Dashwood go with Lady Middleton, their Barton neighbour, to a crowded London party. There Elinor sees Willoughby talking closely with a fashionably dressed young woman; he bows but does not approach. Marianne calls out to him and holds out her hand. He comes over, speaks coldly to Elinor rather than to her, barely touches her hand, and says only that he called in Berkeley Street and left his card. When Marianne begs to know what is wrong and whether he had her letters, he turns back to his companion. Marianne nearly faints, and Lady Middleton takes them home. Elinor concludes that Willoughby has tired of whatever tie existed.

Before dawn Marianne Dashwood, staying in London with Mrs. Jennings, writes in tears to Willoughby. At breakfast his reply arrives. Mrs. Jennings, their hostess, cheerfully asks Elinor Dashwood when the wedding will be; Elinor denies any engagement. Upstairs she finds Marianne sobbing with the letter: Willoughby coldly regrets if his behaviour misled her, says his affections have long been engaged elsewhere and that he will soon be married, and returns her letters and lock of hair. Elinor is disgusted. Marianne admits they were never engaged, and that he never said in so many words that he loved her, though she felt bound to him. She blames others, not him, and begs to go home to their mother.

Mrs. Jennings, the Dashwood sisters' hostess in London, comes home full of the news: Willoughby is to marry a Miss Grey, who has fifty thousand pounds. She pities Marianne Dashwood loudly and tries to comfort her with sweetmeats, a good fire and old Constantia wine, which Elinor Dashwood drinks herself. Marianne sits through dinner in silence and goes early to bed. Mrs. Jennings predicts that Colonel Brandon, their friend from Barton, will now marry Marianne by midsummer, and praises his estate, Delaford. Elinor tells her there was no definite engagement. The colonel calls that evening, already having overheard the news in a shop in Pall Mall, and asks anxiously how Marianne bears it.

A letter Mrs. Jennings brings Marianne Dashwood proves to be from her mother, still full of trust in Willoughby, and Marianne weeps afresh. Colonel Brandon, their friend, calls and tells Elinor Dashwood his story. As a young man he loved Eliza, his father's ward, who was forced to marry his brother; ill-treated, she was divorced and sank into ruin, and he found her dying in a debtors' house. She left him her small daughter, also Eliza, whom he had educated. Last February the girl, then about sixteen, vanished from Bath. Her letter in October called him from Barton: Willoughby had seduced her and left her pregnant and without help. Brandon and Willoughby fought a duel; neither was hurt.

Elinor Dashwood tells her sister Marianne what Colonel Brandon revealed about Willoughby. Marianne believes it, no longer defends him and treats the colonel more gently, but is as dejected as ever. Their mother writes that they should stay in London rather than return to Barton, partly because their half-brother John Dashwood will be in town in February. Sir John Middleton, Mrs. Palmer and Mrs. Jennings rage against Willoughby; Lady Middleton is politely indifferent. Early in February Elinor tells Marianne that Willoughby has married Miss Grey and left town. The Miss Steeles, Anne and Lucy, arrive in London to stay with cousins in Holborn; Lucy, secretly engaged to Edward Ferrars, needles Elinor about being still in town.

Marianne Dashwood goes out for the first time since her disappointment, with her sister Elinor and their hostess Mrs. Jennings, to Gray's the jeweller. They wait while a conceited, fashionable young man fusses over ordering a toothpick case. There they meet their half-brother, John Dashwood, newly arrived in London with his wife Fanny. He calls next day, and walking with Elinor to visit Sir John and Lady Middleton he urges her to secure Colonel Brandon, whom he takes for her suitor. He mentions that Fanny's mother, Mrs. Ferrars, plans to marry her son Edward to a Miss Morton, a lord's daughter with thirty thousand pounds. He pleads poverty despite buying land and improving Norland, and hopes Mrs. Jennings will leave his sisters money.

Fanny Dashwood, wife of the Dashwood sisters' half-brother John, calls on Mrs. Jennings and Lady Middleton and takes to the latter. The John Dashwoods give a dinner in Harley Street. Elinor and Marianne Dashwood come with Mrs. Jennings; the Middletons bring their guests Anne and Lucy Steele; Colonel Brandon is there, but Fanny's brother Edward Ferrars is not. Elinor at last meets his mother, Mrs. Ferrars, a small, sour, proud woman who snubs her pointedly while being gracious to Lucy, not knowing Lucy is secretly engaged to Edward. When Elinor's painted screens are admired, Mrs. Ferrars and Fanny praise Miss Morton's art instead. Marianne angrily defends her sister, then bursts into tears on Elinor's shoulder.

The morning after the Harley Street dinner, Lucy Steele calls on Elinor Dashwood at Mrs. Jennings's house to exult over how kindly Mrs. Ferrars, the mother of her secret fiancé Edward Ferrars, treated her. Elinor points out that Mrs. Ferrars does not know of the engagement. Edward himself is then announced and walks in on the two of them. All three are painfully embarrassed; Lucy stays silent and watchful while Elinor makes conversation, then fetches her sister. Marianne Dashwood greets Edward with open affection, praises his conscience and scruples about keeping promises, and hints that Lucy should go. Edward leaves quickly and Lucy soon after. Marianne is puzzled; Elinor, bound to secrecy, cannot explain.

Charlotte Palmer, daughter of the Dashwood sisters' London hostess Mrs. Jennings, gives birth to a son, and Mrs. Jennings spends her days with her. Elinor and Marianne Dashwood therefore pass their time with Lady Middleton and her guests, Anne and Lucy Steele, who do not want them. Their sister-in-law Fanny Dashwood is obliged to take them to a musical party, where Elinor is introduced to Robert Ferrars, Edward's younger brother: he is the conceited man she saw choosing a toothpick case, and talks foolishly about cottages. John Dashwood proposes inviting his sisters to stay in Harley Street; Fanny instead invites the Miss Steeles. Lucy shows Elinor the note in triumph, and the Steeles become great favourites there.

Mrs. Jennings, the Dashwood sisters' hostess in London, brings news: Anne Steele has blurted out to Fanny Dashwood that her sister Lucy is secretly engaged to Fanny's brother Edward Ferrars. Fanny fell into hysterics and turned both Steeles out of her Harley Street house. Elinor Dashwood now tells her sister Marianne the truth, and that she has known it for four months; Marianne, astonished and ashamed of her own conduct, promises self-control. Next day their half-brother John Dashwood reports that Mrs. Ferrars, Edward's mother, offered him an estate if he would marry Miss Morton and threatened him with poverty otherwise. Edward refused to give up Lucy, was cast off, and has left the house; the estate is to be settled on his brother Robert.

On a fine March Sunday Elinor Dashwood walks in Kensington Gardens with Mrs. Jennings, her London hostess, and meets Anne Steele. Anne, who listened at the door, relates what passed between her sister Lucy and Edward Ferrars after his mother disowned him: Edward said that, having only two thousand pounds, he would release Lucy if she wished; Lucy refused to give him up. He means to become a clergyman, is lodging in Pall Mall and may go to Oxford, and they will marry when he gets a living. Elinor rebukes Anne for eavesdropping. Next morning Lucy writes to Elinor with the same account, hinting that friends might find Edward a living; Mrs. Jennings reads the letter aloud with approval.

After more than two months in London, Marianne Dashwood longs to go home. The Palmers, the daughter and son-in-law of their hostess Mrs. Jennings, invite the sisters to travel with them to Cleveland, their house in Somersetshire, at Easter; from there Barton is a day's journey. Marianne recoils from the county of Willoughby's home, but Elinor Dashwood persuades her. Colonel Brandon, their friend, then speaks privately with Elinor: hearing how Edward Ferrars has been cast off for keeping his engagement, he offers him the living of Delaford, worth about two hundred a year, and asks her to tell Edward. He thinks it too small to marry on. Mrs. Jennings, half overhearing, believes he has proposed to Elinor.

Mrs. Jennings, the Dashwood sisters' London hostess, congratulates Elinor Dashwood, believing Colonel Brandon has proposed to her, and the two talk at cross purposes. Elinor sits down to write to Edward Ferrars about the colonel's offer of the Delaford living, but Edward himself comes in to take leave before going to Oxford. Awkwardly she tells him the news. Astonished, he insists he owes it to her; she says it is the colonel's own doing. He goes off to thank Brandon, and Elinor reflects that when she next sees him he will be the husband of Lucy Steele. When Mrs. Jennings returns, her mistake is cleared up; she expects Edward and Lucy at Delaford parsonage before Michaelmas.

Edward Ferrars thanks Colonel Brandon for the Delaford living and tells his fiancée Lucy Steele, who is delighted. Elinor Dashwood calls alone at Harley Street to ask after her sister-in-law Fanny. Her half-brother John Dashwood is amazed that the colonel gave away a living he could have sold, and wants it kept from Mrs. Ferrars, Edward's mother. He says Robert Ferrars is now to marry Miss Morton instead of Edward, and whispers that Mrs. Ferrars would have much preferred Edward's attachment to Elinor to this one. Robert, the younger brother, comes in, laughs at the idea of Edward as a country clergyman and calls Lucy an awkward country girl. Fanny appears and is unusually civil to Elinor.

Early in April Elinor and Marianne Dashwood leave London with Mrs. Jennings, her daughter Charlotte Palmer and the baby, and after three days reach Cleveland, the Palmers' house in Somersetshire. Marianne, conscious of being within thirty miles of Willoughby's Combe Magna, walks alone through the grounds to a hilltop temple and weeps. Rain then keeps the party indoors. Mr. Palmer and Colonel Brandon join them the next day; Elinor finds Mr. Palmer civil at home though idle and selfish, and hears from the colonel about his plans for Delaford parsonage, where Edward Ferrars is to live. Marianne's twilight walks in the long wet grass give her a heavy cold, which she refuses to nurse.

At Cleveland, the Palmers' house in Somersetshire, Marianne Dashwood's cold turns into a fever. The apothecary, Mr. Harris, mentions infection, so Charlotte Palmer leaves with her baby and her husband follows; her mother Mrs. Jennings stays to help Elinor Dashwood nurse, and Colonel Brandon, their friend, remains too. After several days Marianne suddenly worsens and grows delirious, calling for her mother. The colonel sets off at once for Barton to fetch Mrs. Dashwood. After a night and morning of real danger the fever breaks, and Mr. Harris declares Marianne out of danger. That stormy evening Elinor hears a carriage, runs down expecting her mother and the colonel, and finds Willoughby in the drawing room.

Willoughby, the man who courted and then dropped Marianne Dashwood, has driven from London since morning after hearing from Sir John Middleton that she was dying at Cleveland. He begs her sister Elinor to hear him. He admits he first paid court to Marianne out of vanity, then truly loved her and meant to propose; but his relative Mrs. Smith learned of his affair with Eliza, Colonel Brandon's ward, and disowned him, and, deep in debt, he chose to marry the wealthy Miss Grey. In London he avoided the sisters, and his cruel letter was dictated by his jealous fiancée. He is unhappy in his marriage and still loves Marianne. Elinor, softened, pities him and promises to tell Marianne; he leaves.

Left alone at Cleveland after Willoughby's visit, Elinor Dashwood finds herself pitying him more than she thinks he deserves. Soon afterwards Colonel Brandon arrives with her mother, Mrs. Dashwood, who had already been preparing to come and had left the youngest daughter, Margaret, with friends. Elinor meets them with the news that Marianne is out of danger. Marianne mends daily. Mrs. Dashwood confides to Elinor that on the journey the colonel told her he loves Marianne; she is delighted, now thinks his manners better than Willoughby's ever were, and is sure Marianne will be happier with him in time, though he himself has little hope. Elinor wishes him success, yet feels a pang for Willoughby.

Marianne Dashwood recovers quickly at Cleveland and thanks Colonel Brandon, their friend, for fetching her mother. Mrs. Dashwood and her daughters Elinor and Marianne take leave of Mrs. Jennings, who nursed her, and travel home to Barton Cottage in the colonel's carriage; he goes to his own house, Delaford. Marianne is calm and plans a life of study, music and walks. On their first walk she points out the hill where she fell and first saw Willoughby, blames her own conduct, compares it with Elinor's, and says she would be at peace if she knew he had not always been deceiving her. Elinor then tells her of Willoughby's visit and confession. Marianne weeps and asks her to tell their mother.

Mrs. Dashwood hears from her daughter Elinor what Willoughby confessed; she pities him but no longer wishes him for Marianne. That evening Marianne Dashwood says she is satisfied and could never have been happy with him, and Elinor points out that selfishness ruled all his conduct. The youngest sister, Margaret, comes home, and Elinor waits anxiously for news of Edward Ferrars. One day the manservant Thomas returns from Exeter and announces that Mr. Ferrars is married: he saw him in a chaise with Lucy Steele, who said she had changed her name and sent her compliments. Marianne falls into hysterics and Elinor turns pale. Mrs. Dashwood realises how much Elinor has been suffering in silence.

Elinor Dashwood, at Barton Cottage with her mother and sisters, finds that knowing Edward Ferrars is married is far worse than expecting it, and pictures him and Lucy Steele settled at Delaford parsonage. No letter comes. While they look for Colonel Brandon, a rider stops at the gate, and it is Edward himself. He enters pale and uneasy; the family receive him with strained politeness. When Elinor forces herself to ask after Mrs. Edward Ferrars, he answers in confusion that she must mean Mrs. Robert Ferrars: his brother Robert has just married Lucy Steele, and they are at Dawlish. Elinor hurries from the room and bursts into tears of joy. Edward falls silent, then walks out towards the village.

Edward Ferrars, freed by Lucy Steele's marriage to his brother Robert, proposes to Elinor Dashwood at Barton Cottage within hours and is accepted, to the joy of her mother and her sister Marianne. He explains that his engagement to Lucy was an idle boyish attachment, and shows Elinor the letter in which Lucy announced her marriage. They agree that the Delaford living and their small means are not quite enough to marry on. Colonel Brandon, his patron, arrives for a visit and the two men become friends. Letters from Mrs. Jennings and from Elinor's half-brother John Dashwood describe the fury of Mrs. Ferrars, Edward's mother, at Robert. Edward decides to go to London and seek a reconciliation with her.

Mrs. Ferrars, Edward Ferrars's mother, receives him again and, after resisting, consents to his marrying Elinor Dashwood, giving them ten thousand pounds. They marry at Barton church in the autumn and settle at Delaford parsonage, close to Colonel Brandon, Edward's patron. Robert Ferrars and his wife Lucy win back Mrs. Ferrars's favour by flattery and remain her favourites. Elinor's mother, Mrs. Dashwood, and her sisters are often at Delaford, and all of them wish Marianne Dashwood to marry the colonel. In time, at nineteen, she does, and comes to love him wholeheartedly. Willoughby, who once abandoned her, hears of it with regret but lives comfortably enough. Mrs. Dashwood stays at Barton Cottage with Margaret, the youngest daughter, and the families remain close.
